ground_truth_witness: Take f(n) = 3n, g(n) = 2n, M = 1, c_1 = 2 (all exact integers). Every hypothesis of the quoted step holds: g(n) = 2n >= 0 for all n >= 1; f(n) > M*g(n) for all n >= 1 (3n > 2n); and 0 <= M <= c_1 (0 <= 1 <= 2). Yet the asserted conclusion fails at every n >= 1: c_1*g(n) = 2*(2n) = 4n, while f(n) = 3n, so c_1*g(n) = 4n > 3n = f(n). At n = 1: claim says c_1*g(n) <= f(n); here c_1*g(1) = 4 > 3 = f(1). A strictly smaller (degenerate) witness found by exhaustive pointwise search is g = 1, f = 1, M = 0, c_1 = 2: hypotheses 1 >= 0, 1 > 0*1 = 0, 0 <= 0 <= 2 all hold, but c_1*g = 2 > 1 = f. Note f(n) = Omega(g(n)) is nonetheless TRUE in the 3n/2n instance (with the correct constant c_1 = 1 or any c_1 <= 3/2); what the witness refutes is precisely the stated inference "pick c_1 >= M, hence c_1*g(n) <= f(n)". The script also runs a negative control: under the alternative reading in which M is universally quantified (f(n) > M*g(n) for EVERY M >= 0), exhaustive search over the same grid finds 0 violations among 420 hypothesis-satisfying tuples, confirming that the defect is specific to the fixed-M phrasing the sentence actually uses and that instantiating M := c_1 repairs it.
ground_truth_flaw: The Omega-part argument claims that from f(n) > M*g(n), choosing a constant c_1 satisfying 0 <= M <= c_1 yields the relation 0 <= c_1*g(n) <= f(n). This inference has the inequality direction backwards: a constant c_1 >= M does not in general satisfy c_1*g(n) <= f(n); one must pick 0 < c_1 <= M (or instantiate the universally quantified M at c_1). The stated implication is false as written.
